essentialQuestion.source: How would you design an AI helper that is useful, fair and safe?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you design an AI helper that is useful, fair and safe?

learningGoal.source: Learn how two real Southeast Asian projects grew from a shared problem, then plan a helper of your own: who it helps, whether AI fits, how to check it works, and one improvement.
learningGoal.back: Learn how two real projects in Southeast Asia grew from problems people share, then plan your own helper: whom it helps, whether AI fits, how to check that it works, and one improvement.

evidence.cards.0.title.source: Two real projects in Southeast Asia
evidence.cards.0.title.back: Two real projects in Southeast Asia

evidence.cards.0.cases.0.name.source: Eco Pulse, Malaysia: a student prototype
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.name.back: Eco Pulse, Malaysia: a students' prototype

evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.source: The problem: the students wanted to make recycling quicker and easier. Who built it: three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, a secondary school in Johor, for a 2024 student competition run by Samsung with Universiti Malaya. What the AI does: an app looks at a photo of a recyclable item and estimates its weight and value. How far it has got: a prototype, a first working version. The evidence: it won first prize in the competition's recycling category. The organiser says it is precise, but no test results have been published. A question: how well does it work with dirty or crushed items?
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.back: Problem: students wanted to make recycling faster and easier. Who built it: three 15-year-old students from SMK Sultan Ismail, a secondary school in Johor state, for a 2024 student competition Samsung ran with Universiti Malaya. What the AI does: the app looks at a photo of a recyclable item, then estimates its weight and value. Stage reached: a prototype, which is a first working version. Evidence: it won first prize in the competition's recycling category. The organisers say the app is accurate, but no test results have been published. Question: how well does the app work with items that are dirty or squashed flat?
evidence.cards.0.cases.0.body.note: Johor as รัฐยะโฮร์ (not in KEY_TERMS). School and university names (SMK Sultan Ismail, Universiti Malaya) kept in Latin letters.

evidence.cards.0.cases.1.name.source: SELENA+, Singapore: tested, then put to use
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.name.back: SELENA+, Singapore: tested, then put into real use

evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.source: The problem: people with diabetes need regular eye checks, because the illness can harm their eyes, and checking every eye photo takes many trained people. Who built it: eye doctors and scientists at the Singapore Eye Research Institute and the Singapore National Eye Centre, with computer scientists from the National University of Singapore. What the AI does: it looks at photos of the back of the eye and marks the ones an eye specialist should see. How far it has got: in 2017 the team reported tests on about 500,000 eye photos from Singapore and other countries. In 2024 they reported that it was being used in Singapore's national eye-screening programme. The evidence: these are the team's own reports. A question: does it help patients keep their sight? The reports don't say yet.
evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body.back: Problem: people with diabetes need regular eye checks, because the disease can harm the eyes, and checking every eye photo needs many trained people. Who built it: eye doctors and scientists at the Singapore Eye Research Institute and the Singapore National Eye Centre, with computer scientists from the National University of Singapore. What the AI does: it looks at photos of the back of the eye, then marks the photos an expert eye doctor should look at. Stage reached: in 2017 the team reported test results on about 500,000 eye photos from Singapore and other countries. In 2024 the team reported the system is used in Singapore's national eye-screening programme. Evidence: these are the team's own reports. Question: does this system help patients keep their sight? The reports do not say yet.

activity.instructions.source: Plan a helper in five steps. This plan is your main work for the lesson: Write and Speak use it. read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with a problem people share
read.sections.0.heading.back: Start from a problem people share

read.sections.0.text.source: In this project, you will plan a helper for a problem that many people in a community share. Good designers start with the problem and the people it affects, not with the tool. Two real projects from Southeast Asia show how. In Johor, Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier. For a 2024 student competition, they built Eco Pulse, an app that looks at a photo of a recyclable item and estimates its weight and value. In Singapore, people with diabetes need regular eye checks, because the illness can harm their eyes, and checking every photo takes many trained people. Eye doctors and computer scientists there built SELENA+, which looks at photos of the back of the eye and marks the ones a specialist should see.
read.sections.0.text.back: In this project you will plan a helper for a problem many people in a community share. Good designers start from the problem and the people who face it, not from the tool. Two real projects from Southeast Asia show how. In Johor state, Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier. For a 2024 student competition they built Eco Pulse, an app that looks at a photo of a recyclable item, then estimates its weight and value. In Singapore people with diabetes need regular eye checks, because the disease can harm the eyes, and checking every picture needs many trained people. So eye doctors and computer scientists there built SELENA+, which looks at photos of the back of the eye and marks the pictures an expert should look at.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: You will plan a helper for a problem many people share. Good designers start with the problem, not the tool. Here are two real projects. In Johor, Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted easier recycling. They built an app called Eco Pulse. From a photo of an item, it tells its weight and value. In Singapore, people with diabetes need eye checks. The illness can harm their eyes. Checking every photo takes many trained people. Eye doctors and computer scientists built SELENA+. It marks the eye photos that a specialist should see.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: You will plan a helper for a problem many people share. Good designers start from the problem, not from the tool. Here are two real projects. In Johor state, Malaysia, three 15-year-old students wanted to make recycling easier. They built an app called Eco Pulse. The app looks at a picture of an item, then gives its weight and value. In Singapore people with diabetes must get eye checks. The disease can harm the eyes. Checking every picture needs many trained people. Eye doctors and computer scientists built a system called SELENA+. The system marks eye pictures an expert should look at.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How far has a project got?
read.sections.1.heading.back: What stage has the project reached?

read.sections.1.text.source: A project grows in stages, and each stage needs its own evidence. A proposal is an idea on paper. A prototype is a first working version. Testing checks it carefully with new examples it has never seen. Being in use means real people rely on it. Showing impact means there is evidence that it made life better. Eco Pulse won first prize in its category, which shows that judges thought the prototype was strong. It doesn't show how well the app works with dirty or crushed items, or that people use it. SELENA+ has gone further. In 2017, its team reported tests on about 500,000 eye photos from Singapore and other countries. In 2024, they reported that it was being used in Singapore's national eye-screening programme. These are the team's own reports, and they don't yet show whether patients' eyesight is better.
read.sections.1.text.back: Projects grow in stages, and each stage needs its own evidence. A proposal is an idea on paper. A prototype is a first working version. Testing is a careful check with new examples it has never seen. Being put into real use means real people rely on it. Showing impact means there is evidence it makes lives better. Eco Pulse won first prize in its category, which shows the judges thought this prototype was very good, but does not show how well the app works with dirty or squashed items, or that anyone uses this app. SELENA+, on the other hand, has already gone further than that. In 2017 its team reported test results on about 500,000 eye photos from Singapore and other countries. In 2024 the team reported the system is used in Singapore's national eye-screening programme. All this is the team's own reporting, and it has not yet shown whether patients' sight improved.
read.sections.1.text.note: Reviewer: The two sentences ran together (หรือแสดงว่ามีคนใช้ SELENA+ ไปได้ไกลกว่านั้น could be read as “or show that people use SELENA+”). Split with ส่วน so SELENA+ starts a new sentence, as in the English.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A project grows in stages. A proposal is just an idea. A prototype is the first version that works. Testing checks it with new examples. Then real people use it. Last, there may be evidence that it made life better. That is called impact. Eco Pulse won a prize, so judges liked the prototype. That does not show how well it works, or that people use it. SELENA+ has gone further. In 2017, its team tested it on about 500,000 eye photos. In 2024, they said Singapore's eye checks used it. These reports don't show if people can see better.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Projects grow in stages. A proposal is only an idea. A prototype is a first working version. Testing is checking with new examples. Then real people use it. Finally there may be evidence that it makes lives better. This is called impact. The Eco Pulse project won a prize, which means the judges liked this prototype. But that does not show how well it works, or whether anyone uses it. The SELENA+ system has gone further. In 2017 the team tested it on about 500,000 eye photos. In 2024 the team said Singapore's eye checks use this system. These reports do not show whether people see better.

read.sections.2.text.source: Now it's your turn. First, decide whether AI should be used at all. AI can help when a helper must recognise or guess from many examples, like items in photos or signs of eye disease. But a sign, a simple rule or a person can be a better answer, and a well-explained simpler plan is a strong design. Then plan what your helper would learn from, what could go wrong and who would check it. Like SELENA+, it should be tested with examples it has never seen, from the people who will use it. Finally, look at your plan again, or listen to feedback. Designers change a plan and test it again. This is called iteration. Change one thing, and you have version 2.
read.sections.2.text.back: Now it is your turn. First decide whether to use AI. AI helps when the helper needs to recognise or guess from many examples, such as items in photos or signs of eye disease. But a sign, a simple rule or a person may be a better answer, and a simpler plan with its reasons well explained is good design. Then plan what your helper will learn from, what could go wrong and who will check it. Like SELENA+, a helper should be tested with examples it has never seen, from the people who will really use it. Finally look at your plan again or listen to feedback. Designers change the plan and test again; this is called iteration. Change one thing, and you will have version 2.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Should AI be used at all? AI can help when a helper must learn from many examples. But a sign, a rule or a person can be better. A simpler plan is fine, with reasons. Plan what it learns from, what could go wrong, and who checks it. Test it with new examples from its users. Then look at your plan again, or get feedback. Change it and test again. This is called iteration. Change one thing for version 2.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Should it use AI? AI helps when the helper must learn from many examples. But a sign, a rule or a person may be better. A simpler plan is fine too, if it has reasons. Plan what it learns from, what could go wrong and who checks. Test with new examples from the people who will use it. Then look at the plan again or ask for feedback. Change the plan and test again. This is called iteration. Change one thing to make version 2.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon goes over the basics of AI. AI tools learn from training data. This is a large set of examples that helps them find patterns and make guesses. Some AI tools sort things or make guesses about them. Other tools, called generative AI, make new things, like writing or pictures. The video explains that AI can be very useful, but it is not perfect. It learns from what people give it, so it can repeat their mistakes. That is why the people who make and use AI need to be responsible. They need to check its answers and think about who it might affect. This is a good review before you design your own AI helper.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon reviews the basics of AI. AI tools learn from training data, a large set of examples that helps them find patterns and guess. Some AI tools group things or make guesses about them. Other tools, called generative AI, create new things such as writing or pictures. The video explains that AI can be very useful but is not perfect. It learns from what people give it, so it can repeat the same mistakes people make. This is why people who build and use AI must be responsible: they must check its answers and think about whom it might affect. This is a good review before you design your own AI helper.

educatorNotes.0.source: This is a design on paper: nothing is built, and coding is optional. The plan is the lesson's single working document: Write asks what stage it has reached and what evidence it would need, Speak presents it, and step 5 revises it once; no second plan is asked for. Assess five things, not how impressive or how wary the plan sounds: the need (a real problem and who it affects), the intended benefit, technical fit (why AI helps, why another way fits better, or what the learner still needs to find out: all three are strong answers), evidence and checks (how they would test it with unseen examples, and who checks), and one improvement. It covers UNESCO's AI system design aspect at the Understand level and touches Create. Paper version: the five steps as a worksheet. Older or more confident learners can add a test plan (which new examples, and what result would count as working).

educatorNotes.1.source: The two real projects, and how far each has got. Eco Pulse is known only from its organiser's account (Samsung Malaysia, 11 December 2024, re-read 8 November 2026): team “Terralnnovators” (so spelled), three 15-year-olds at SMK Sultan Ismail, Johor, with an “AI-driven image recognition app” that estimates the value and weight of recyclable items; first prize in the Accessible Recycling category of Solve for Tomorrow 2024 (with Universiti Malaya; final 7 December 2024), where finalists presented prototypes. “With precision” is the organiser's claim; no test results, users or deployment are reported. SELENA+: developed and validated by SERI/SNEC with NUS computer scientists (Ting and others, JAMA, December 2017: 494,661 retinal images; primary validation in Singapore's national diabetic retinopathy screening programme, 14,880 patients; 10 further multiethnic datasets; “further research is necessary” in health care settings). Deployment comes from a separate source, the developers' own case study (Gunasekeran and others, NEJM AI, November 2024): SELENA+ in the Singapore Integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Programme with medical-device approval; in a pilot of the first 1,712 patients it was less sensitive and less specific than human graders for referable retinopathy (94.7% and 82.2%, against 98.9% and 97.2%) and more sensitive for vision-threatening retinopathy. Not an independent evaluation, and no patient outcomes. Don't attribute Lesson 10's made-up Sunvale eye helper's weaknesses to SELENA+.
educatorNotes.1.back: The two real projects and the stage each has reached. Eco Pulse is known only from the organisers' account (Samsung Malaysia, 11 December 2024, reread 8 November 2026): team “Terralnnovators” (spelled like this), three 15-year-old students at SMK Sultan Ismail, Johor, with an “AI-powered image recognition app” estimating the value and weight of recyclables, won first prize in the Accessible Recycling category of Solve for Tomorrow 2024 (with Universiti Malaya; final on 7 December 2024), where finalists presented prototypes. “Accurate” is the organisers' claim; no test results, users or real deployment are reported. SELENA+ was developed and validated by SERI/SNEC with NUS computer scientists (Ting et al., JAMA, December 2017: 494,661 retinal images; main validation in Singapore's national diabetic retinopathy screening programme, 14,880 patients; 10 more multi-ethnic datasets; and “further research is needed” in healthcare settings). Information on real use comes from another source, the developers' own case study (Gunasekeran et al., NEJM AI, November 2024): SELENA+ is in the Singapore Integrated Diabetic Retinopathy Programme and approved as a medical device. In a pilot with the first 1,712 patients, the system had lower sensitivity and specificity than human graders for referable retinopathy (94.7 and 82.2 percent versus 98.9 and 97.2 percent) and higher sensitivity for sight-threatening retinopathy. This is not an independent evaluation, and there are no patient outcome data. Do not carry over the weaknesses of the fictional Sunvale eye-checking helper in Lesson 10 to SELENA+.
